Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) totally fun first (i.e., Entertainment game reappropriated), 
        (2) mostly fun first (i.e., design workshop with disabled stakeholders),
        (3) both fun and utility first (i.e., design workshop with diverse stakeholders), 
        (4) mostly utility first (i.e., primary utilitarian mechanic designed first),
        (5) totally utility first (i.e., made by clinicians or specialists, fun incorporated later)
reasoning: The study explicitly states it used an "iterative and interdisciplinary design approach" (chunk_24, chunk_1) to "reconcile clinical requirements with game design for player engagement" (chunk_24, chunk_19). It also mentions placing "the same emphasis on game design and player motivation as it does on therapeutic requirements" (chunk_8). The design process involved an "interdisciplinary appraisal" where "clinical importance was weighted against the virtualization complexity and potential of the feature" and the "motivational pull of the game" was discussed (chunk_11). This indicates both fun (player engagement/motivation) and utility (clinical requirements/therapeutic protocols) were considered equally and from the beginning by diverse stakeholders.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) unstructured play (i.e., no rules, making art),
        (2) semi-structured play (i.e., playground activities),
        (3) flexible structure with rules (i.e., improv),
        (4) flexible game (i.e., board game with house rules),
        (5) game with rigid rules (i.e., video game)
reasoning: The study describes a game called RollAbility, which is an "open-world, medieval-themed game" where players can "drive around freely" and have a "choice of mission" and "free movement in between exercises." This indicates flexibility. However, the game design is also "based upon standardized training methods" from the "Wheelchair Skills Program manual" which defines "clinical standards regarding the training setup, and grading," and tasks are "set and evaluated to meet clinically relevant criteria." This indicates a structured, rule-based foundation. The combination of standardized rules with an open-world environment and player choice best fits the description of a flexible game.

        (3) equally skill and chance-based (i.e., catan),
        (4) mostly chance-based (i.e., Uno),

reasoning: The game 'RollAbility' is explicitly designed around 'Wheelchair Skills Program (WSP) tasks' that 'require the player to perform a specifc skill' to improve wheelchair skill. While one example mission mentions 'fshing with a chance of catching random objects', the primary objective and design of the game are focused on skill-based training, making it mostly skill-based.

        (1) entirely solo (i.e., solitaire),
        (2) mostly solo (i.e., playing against AI in single-player StarCraft),
        (3) mix of solo and social affordances (i.e., animal crossing),
        (4) mostly social, but aspects are independent (i.e., house on hill haunt transition),
        (5) entirely social (i.e., tag)
reasoning: The game 'RollAbility' is described as an open-world game where a single player drives freely, completes missions, and interacts with Non Playable Characters (NPCs). There is no mention of multiplayer or social interaction with other human players. This design, involving a single player interacting with AI (NPCs) in a virtual world, best fits the 'mostly solo' category.

Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely turn-based (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) follows a set of steps (i.e., viticulture's dynamic turn ordering),
        (3) turns are taken, but some actions can be taken at any time (i.e., pandemic),
        (4) most actions can be taken at any time, but there are some phases (i.e., PvP death reset timer),
        (5) entirely simultaneous (i.e., race)
reasoning: The context describes RollAbility as an "open-world game in which the player can drive around freely." Players can choose when to start specific "missions" and can "drive around freely and choose a new mission" after completion. This indicates that most actions (free movement) can be taken at any time, with missions representing structured phases.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely competitive (i.e., spit card game),
        (2) mostly competitive, but sometimes collaboration is important (i.e., forbidden island),
        (3) mix of competitive and collaborative (i.e., mario party 2 vs 2 mini-games),
        (4) mostly collaborative (i.e., animal crossing),
        (5) entirely collaborative (i.e., pandemic)
reasoning: The study describes a single-player game designed for individual wheelchair skills training for children with Cerebral Palsy. The game implements therapeutic exercises as interactive missions, focusing on player engagement and motivation through rewards and varied gameplay. There is no mention of competitive elements or interaction with other players. Therefore, the game is entirely focused on the player working with the game system to achieve personal therapeutic goals, making it entirely non-competitive and aligning best with an "entirely collaborative" design in the context of the provided options, where the player "collaborates" with the game system for their own benefit.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely symmetrical (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) mostly symmetrical (i.e., undertale's differing NPC behaviors based on previous playthroughs),
        (3) both symmetrical and asymmetrical (i.e., pandemic with its similar turn structure but different character abilities),
        (4) mostly asymmetrical (i.e., tag),
        (5) entirely asymmetrical (i.e., keep talking, nobody explodes)
reasoning: The game 'RollAbility' features both symmetrical and asymmetrical elements. The core therapeutic tasks are standardized and can be repetitive, representing a symmetrical structure. However, the game also includes asymmetrical aspects such as an open-world environment, free movement, player choice of missions (once unlocked), random rewards, varied in-game tasks and visuals across different levels, and adaptive exercise difficulty adjusted by the therapist.
